newsitem.title: USA: Reebok shareholders vote to cut board terms.
newsitem.headline: Reebok shareholders vote to cut board terms.

text.p: Reebok International Ltd shareholders voted 53 percent in favor Thursday of a CalPERS proposal to cut terms for directors to one year from three.
Reebok Chief Executive Paul Fireman told Reuters following the meeting that the board of directors would take the vote under consideration.

The California Public Employees' Retirement System (CalPERS), which owns about 599,000 shares, put forward the proposal to urge the board to eliminate the "classified board," whereby directors serve three year terms and one-third of the board are up for election at a given time.
CalPERS said in its supporting statement in the Reebok proxy form that a classified board "insulates its members from immediate challenge" and hampers accountability.
"It's certainly not an overwhemling majority, but we will take it into consideration," Fireman told Reuters after the company's annual meeting in Boston.
But Fireman said he remains opposed to adopting a classified board.

"I think the staggered board (with three-year terms) is much, much in the best interests of the shareholders," Fireman said. "I think it will realize for them the best value in any way we go forward."

Fireman said the classified board with one-year terms may be in the interests of institutional shareholders when there is a takeover of a company and the directors can be quickly voted out of office all at once.
But he added, "there is no takeover talk," of Reebok.

Peter Russ, an analyst from Shelby, Collum, Davis and Co who represents some institutional customers, said the shareholder vote should serve as a warning to Reebok management that shareholders are dissatisfied.
"Thank God for CalPERS," he said. "That's very unusual. That's a real sign of shareholder unrest."

CalPERS, the nation's largest public pension fund, said in February it would target Reebok and nine other companies and warned the board of directors could face a fight for reelection if they do not improve performance.
The pension fund said in February that Reebok has been in a "financial free fall" and that management has operated with "insufficient accountability" to the board.

Fireman, who told disgruntled shareholders last year that he would step aside in two years if the company did not turn around, said in a speech that athletic footwear sales are strengthening, inventories are in good shape and apparel and leisure shoe sales are growing.

"I do believe we are a much different company than we were a year ago," Fireman said. "We are clearly heading in the right direction, we have a lot of work to do. By no means have we accomplished all the results."
